ECE 6390 / Navigation

Earth-fixed coordinates

From the figure to the physics

Fig. 1 shows the coordinate transformation needed to compare an Earth station with a satellite position.

An Earth-fixed coordinate system rotates with the planet. In a spherical approximation, geocentric latitude L, longitude λ and radius R+h give x = (R+h)cosL cosλ, y = (R+h)cosL sinλ, z = (R+h)sinL.

Rotating this vector about the polar axis by the Earth angle gives a simplified inertial representation. The point has the same physical position and radius, while its coordinate components depend on the reference frame.

For actual navigation, use a consistent terrestrial reference frame, ellipsoidal geodetic coordinates, satellite ephemeris epoch and signal transmission time. The Earth rotates while a signal travels; sufficiently precise ranging must account for that effect.

Example

At zero latitude, zero longitude and zero height, the spherical Earth-fixed coordinates are (R,0,0). After a +90° rotation about z, the inertial coordinates are (0,R,0). The radius is unchanged.

    Practice

    1. Which Cartesian component changes sign when latitude changes from +30° to −30° at fixed longitude and radius?

    Cosine is even; sine is odd.

    z changes sign. x and y remain the same because cos(+30°) = cos(−30°).

    2. Why must station and satellite vectors share both a frame and an epoch before subtraction?

    Subtraction assumes the same coordinate basis at the same instant.

    Different frames or epochs mix rotation and motion into the coordinate difference. Transform both positions consistently before interpreting their difference as a physical line-of-sight vector.
